claims.text: Replacing conventional EAM references with an ab initio-trained deep-learning potential will improve reference–target phase-space overlap for high-temperature multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
Traditional EAM references inadequately represent the broad range of atomic configurations in ab initio liquids of multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
A DeepMD-type potential can be trained on DFT configurations to describe both liquid and solid high-entropy carbonitrides.
Training should use ab initio configurations sampled from both the liquid and high-temperature solid phases of each target alloy.
The proposed method applies primarily to refractory high-entropy alloys and analogous high-entropy compounds near melting.
The applicable temperature range is approximately 0.9 to 1.1 times the melting temperature.
Systems in this temperature range exhibit substantial liquid-like configurational complexity.
The deep-learning potential can represent diverse configurations in both the liquid and high-temperature solid phases.
Representing these configurations makes the reference potential's sampled phase space more similar to that of the ab initio target.
The machine-learning potential accurately reproduces the local environments and energy landscape found in ab initio simulations.
Improved reproduction of the ab initio energy landscape enhances phase-space overlap and reduces thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD EAM references.
The intervention will reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch by roughly 30–50% compared with TOR-TILD EAM references.
Reducing path mismatch will make thermodynamic predictions more reliable and computationally efficient.
Conventional EAM potentials used in TOR-TILD produce large integration-path mismatch because they poorly represent configurations in the ab initio liquid.
The method's benefits will be less pronounced for elemental or binary systems far from melting and for compositions with little high-temperature disorder.
The achieved reduction in integration-path mismatch will depend on alloy composition and the quality and extent of the ab initio training data.
A controlled comparison of EAM and deep-learning references can test the hypothesis using path-mismatch and phase-space-overlap metrics near melting.
Failure to achieve at least a 30% statistically significant reduction in path mismatch, together with no improvement in phase-space overlap, would falsify the hypothesis.
